item.title: How world champion Smith can become a mainstream star
item.description: Dalton Smith made his professional debut in 2019 [Getty Images] Briton Dalton Smith defends his WBC light-welterweight title against Dominican Republic's Alberto Puello on Saturday after stunning Subriel Matias in January . Former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew explains why an Adam Azim fight at Hillsborough could make Smith a household name. Dalton Smith has everything it takes to become British boxing's next superstar. He's one of the best fighters in this country, pound-for-pound, and I'd even go as far as saying he's a better boxer than I ever was. But there's a difference between being a brilliant fighter and becoming a household name. I know that from my own career. My old mate David Haye was the fighter who took my popularity to another level entirely. The whole country thought I was going to get knocked out, but the British public love an underdog story and when I woke up the morning after beating Haye for the first time, my profile had exploded. Suddenly, grandmothers were stopping me in the street telling me they wanted me to punch his head in. Everybody had an opinion. Dalton needs his own Haye - that rival who takes him from being known among boxing fans to being recognised by the whole country. Adam Azim could be that man. It's a rivalry which has been brewing for years and I'd love to see them fight at Sheffield Wednesday's Hillsborough Stadium. It would be a monster fight. But before any of that, Dalton has a massive job to do against Alberto Puello on Saturday. A defeat would be a massive blow for British boxing because this kid is one of the brightest lights we've got. What makes Smith so special? I've known about Dalton since his days on the Great Britain amateur squad. I was surprised he didn't stay amateur for the Olympics because I fancied him to win a medal. But look at him now. Dalton isn't somebody who says outrageous things like Tyson Fury or creates controversy like Derek Chisora. He does his talking in the ring and I respect that. He showed us just how good he was by dethroning the much-feared Matias in New York. I told Eddie Hearn on the morning of the fight that Dalton would stop him. Eddie couldn't believe it, but I was absolutely convinced. It was a phenomenal performance, but what makes Dalton so special is his timing. He reminds me of another brilliant Sheffield fighter, Kell Brook. He's not necessarily the strongest, quickest or sharpest, but technically he does everything really well. He catches opponents in the middle of exchanges with perfect timing. I admire his relationship with his father and trainer, Grant, who has allowed Dalton to travel and learn from different trainers. item.content:encoded: Dalton Smith made his professional debut in 2019 [Getty Images] Briton Dalton Smith defends his WBC light-welterweight title against Dominican Republic's Alberto Puello on Saturday after stunning Subriel Matias in January . Former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew explains why an Adam Azim fight at Hillsborough could make Smith a household name. Dalton Smith has everything it takes to become British boxing's next superstar. He's one of the best fighters in this country, pound-for-pound, and I'd even go as far as saying he's a better boxer than I ever was. But there's a difference between being a brilliant fighter and becoming a household name. I know that from my own career. My old mate David Haye was the fighter who took my popularity to another level entirely. The whole country thought I was going to get knocked out, but the British public love an underdog story and when I woke up the morning after beating Haye for the first time, my profile had exploded. Suddenly, grandmothers were stopping me in the street telling me they wanted me to punch his head in. Everybody had an opinion. Dalton needs his own Haye - that rival who takes him from being known among boxing fans to being recognised by the whole country. Adam Azim could be that man. It's a rivalry which has been brewing for years and I'd love to see them fight at Sheffield Wednesday's Hillsborough Stadium. It would be a monster fight. But before any of that, Dalton has a massive job to do against Alberto Puello on Saturday. A defeat would be a massive blow for British boxing because this kid is one of the brightest lights we've got. What makes Smith so special? I've known about Dalton since his days on the Great Britain amateur squad. I was surprised he didn't stay amateur for the Olympics because I fancied him to win a medal. But look at him now. Dalton isn't somebody who says outrageous things like Tyson Fury or creates controversy like Derek Chisora. He does his talking in the ring and I respect that. He showed us just how good he was by dethroning the much-feared Matias in New York. I told Eddie Hearn on the morning of the fight that Dalton would stop him. Eddie couldn't believe it, but I was absolutely convinced. It was a phenomenal performance, but what makes Dalton so special is his timing. He reminds me of another brilliant Sheffield fighter, Kell Brook. He's not necessarily the strongest, quickest or sharpest, but technically he does everything really well. He catches opponents in the middle of exchanges with perfect timing. I admire his relationship with his father and trainer, Grant, who has allowed Dalton to travel and learn from different trainers. I've had coaches who wouldn't entertain bringing somebody else in to help. Grant understands that no trainer knows everything and Dalton has benefited enormously from that. Puello is Smith's toughest fight yet People are overlooking Puello, which is dangerous. Even though Matias beat him, I genuinely believe this is the toughest fight of Dalton's career. He's a southpaw with a phenomenal work rate and a granite chin. I've hardly ever seen him badly hurt. But Puello is easier to hit than most southpaws because he doesn't use his stance particularly well. I wish I'd faced a few like that during my career – unfortunately, I had to deal with some southpaw guy called Oleksandr Usyk. My only slight concern for Dalton is his work rate. He can't afford to start slowly or he could find himself four or five rounds behind. He must approach every round as a new fight. Don't go looking for the knockout. Go in there looking to win eight, nine or 10 rounds. If he stops Puello, I'll regard him as clearly the best fighter in the division. Even beating him on points would be a brilliant achievement. Afterwards, I don't want to see him jumping through weight divisions chasing big names. Marvin Hagler showed you can become a legend by dominating one division. Stay at light-welterweight, unify the belts and make everybody come to you. Smith v Azim would be electric Dalton Smith (left) is undefeated in 19 professional bouts, winning 14 by stoppage [Getty Images] Dalton has already achieved his dream of becoming world champion. Nobody can ever take that WBC green-and-gold belt away from him. I know he dreams of fighting at Hillsborough and I understand exactly what that means. Winning the WBC title at Goodison Park, the former home of my beloved Everton, was my lifelong dream, which I achieved by knocking out Ilunga Makabu in 2016. Dalton needs the right opponent for his own special night and to make him into a mainstream star. There are huge names out there and Dalton is capable of competing with the very best. But for me, Azim would be the one. There is nothing quite like a domestic rivalry and the atmosphere would be incredible. Two top British fighters, a genuine rivalry and promoters Hearn and Ben Shalom going at each other in the build-up. Azim is lightning fast, possibly the quickest fighter in British boxing pound-for-pound. But timing beats speed, and that's what makes this rivalry so fascinating. I'd love Azim to win a world title first, then they could meet in a unification fight. It could even become a trilogy. But beating Puello is no formality and Dalton cannot afford to lose focus. Then we can start dreaming about Azim and Hillsborough. Tony Bellew was speaking to BBC Sport boxing journalist Kal Sajad. item.title: Stephen A. Smith labels Chiefs star ‘next level’ as he shares impressive stat projection
item.description: Photo by Jason Mendez/Getty Images for SiriusXM Stephen A. Smith has been full of praise for Kansas City Chiefs star Kenneth Walker III this week. Walker joined the Chiefs earlier this year on the back of being named the 2026 Super Bowl MVP for the Seattle Seahawks. He has carried that excellent form into the new season and has helped the 5-0 Chiefs get back to their best after a disappointing 2025/26. Now, when speaking alongside Michael Irvin on the ‘Stephen A. Smith Sports’ YouTube channel, Smith called Walker ‘next level’ and shared that he is currently on course to rush for over 2,200 yards this season. He said: “When I think about newcomers, I think about two people that stand out in my mind. Mike Evans in San Francisco, even though he just got hurt this past Monday night. “And I’m thinking about K9, Kenneth Walker III, for the Kansas City Chiefs. Do you realise that right now Kenneth Walker III is on pace to run, to rush for over 2,200 yards and he’s on pace to have over 2,500 yards from scrimmage this year. This brother is a next-level kind of stud right now.” If he were to keep up that pace for all of this campaign, he would break the record for single-season rushing yards in the NFL during the regular season (2,105 in 1984). But for now, Walker should be focused on facing his former team for the first time this week as the Chiefs aim to extend their unbeaten run to six games. item.title: Ligue 1 Predictions | Round 8: PSG host Lyon, Davide Ancelotti’s Lille travel to Monaco
item.description: Ligue 1 Predictions | Round 8: PSG host Lyon, Davide Ancelotti’s Lille travel to Monaco Ligue 1 Predictions, Round 8 GFFN editor-in-chief Luke Entwistle, and sub-editor Bastien Cheval face off in our Ligue 1 predictions competition, which returns for the 2026/27 campaign. This season, GFFN will also be hosting guests. It’s three points for a correct score, two points for a correct score difference, and one point for a correct result. Who will come out on top at the end of the season? Scores: Luke: 42 Bastien: 27 Game of the week: Paris Saint-Germain v Olympique Lyonnais, Sunday 19:45 (UK) Let’s see if this game actually goes ahead in its allotted slot. There is talk of moving the game to Saturday as a result of the expected protests on Sunday. That, coupled with an NFL game in the city on the same night, is leading to fear that security services may be spread thin. In any case, Paris Saint-Germain are the strong favourites here, naturally. They have just beaten Manchester City and Barcelona in consecutive weeks. They have also rediscovered form in Ligue 1, winning all of their last four in the league. Largely, however, those performances have been unconvincing and Luis Enrique must now contend with the absences of Khvicha Kvaratkshelia, Ousmane Dembélé, and Marquinhos. The former may be out until the end of the season. The other two are also big misses. PSG have the strength and depth to absorb those absences. Désiré Doué has been in red-hot form, whilst Maghnes Akliouche also looks to have turned a corner after a difficult start. But more than ever, there is a dependence on a second-string that has so far struggled. Against Le Mans FC and RC Strasbourg Alsace, Luis Enrique has called in the cavalry around the hour mark to bail his side out. He won’t be able to do that to quite the same extent against Olympique Lyonnais. Whilst OL sit top of the league, their form has dipped slightly this week. They were lucky to take all three points at home to OGC Nice and they were then completely outplayed by Hoffenheim in the UEFA Europa League on Thursday. Lyon also come in less rested, while there remain doubts Paulo Fonseca’s management in these big games. Luke’s Ligue 1 predictions Brest 1-2 Nice Lens 0-2 Paris FC Monaco 2-0 Lille Auxerre 2-1 Le Mans Marseille 1-0 Le Havre Angers 0-3 Lorient Toulouse 4-1 Troyes Rennes 1-1 Strasbourg PSG 3-1 Lyon Bastien’s predictions Brest 2-0 Nice Lens 1-2 Paris FC Monaco 1-0 Lille Angers 1-3 Lorient Auxerre 1-0 Le Mans Marseille 2-0 Le Havre Rennes 2-2 Strasbourg Toulouse 2-0 Troyes PSG 2-1 Lyon GFFN | Luke Entwistle

item.title: Alexander Volkanovski is at a tipping point – here’s the Movsar Evloev plan to push him over the edge
item.description: For all the focus on jabs, elbows, knees and throws, sometimes all it takes is a little push in MMA. Especially when you’re on the precipice. That’s where Alexander Volkanovski finds himself, as much as in Abu Dhabi and at the Etihad Arena . People can talk down the physical threat of Movsar Evloev – and they have – based on the Russian’s relative lack of finishes , but Volkanovski stands on the edge of a sheer drop. It is a long way down, even for the man who walks out to “Down Under”. And this is perhaps the greatest threat to the Australian’s second reign as UFC featherweight champion, at 38 years old. Volkanovski has been one of the finest fighters of a generation, and is arguably the greatest featherweight of all time ( even if the Jose Aldo debate may never end ), but there exists a trend that even the sacred few atop the MMA mountain have been able to outfight or outthink. Alexander Volkanovski ahead of his most-recent fight, a second straight win over Diego Lopes (Getty) “Curse” would be a funner phrasing than trend, and if you want to buy into that framing, it’s a curse that befell the great Anderson Silva, and Israel Adesanya more and Kamaru Usman more recently. Silva held the longest UFC title run of all time, a record he still holds, before being dethroned by Chris Weidman, and that loss kickstarted a 1-7 run that ended his MMA career (barring a no-contest against Nick Diaz, a win that was overturned as Silva failed a drug test). Silva’s broken leg in his rematch with Weidman offers some explanation for his severe drop-off in form, but it cannot wholly account for the skid. One of those to defeat Silva in that miserable middleweight run was Adesanya, who was 22-1, unbeaten at middleweight, and held five successful title defences before his own prime ended in a flash – almost a blur, like his trademark offence during his glory years. Adesanya’s KO by Alex Pereira marked the start of the end; although he avenged that loss with his own KO of the Brazilian five months later, the rematch seemingly showed the last vibrant flicker from a fading fighting light, because he has since lost four in a row – a points loss to seismic underdog Sean Strickland, a submission by Dricus Du Plessis, and KOs by Nassourdine Imavov and Joe Pyfer. Each of the 37-year-old’s opponents was ranked lower than the last. Usman’s decline has felt less drastic, but partly due to his lower in-ring activity, one could argue. The 39-year-old is 1-4 in his last five, like Adesanya, but the latter’s last five fights date back to April 2023, while Usman’s reach back to November 2021. When the welterweight’s 19-fight win streak (including five successful title defences) was ended by Leon Edwards’s iconic head kick, Usman was left lying on his back and sitting in the middle of a 1,316-day wait for a win. item.content:encoded: For all the focus on jabs, elbows, knees and throws, sometimes all it takes is a little push in MMA. Especially when you’re on the precipice. That’s where Alexander Volkanovski finds himself, as much as in Abu Dhabi and at the Etihad Arena . People can talk down the physical threat of Movsar Evloev – and they have – based on the Russian’s relative lack of finishes , but Volkanovski stands on the edge of a sheer drop. It is a long way down, even for the man who walks out to “Down Under”. And this is perhaps the greatest threat to the Australian’s second reign as UFC featherweight champion, at 38 years old. Volkanovski has been one of the finest fighters of a generation, and is arguably the greatest featherweight of all time ( even if the Jose Aldo debate may never end ), but there exists a trend that even the sacred few atop the MMA mountain have been able to outfight or outthink. Alexander Volkanovski ahead of his most-recent fight, a second straight win over Diego Lopes (Getty) “Curse” would be a funner phrasing than trend, and if you want to buy into that framing, it’s a curse that befell the great Anderson Silva, and Israel Adesanya more and Kamaru Usman more recently. Silva held the longest UFC title run of all time, a record he still holds, before being dethroned by Chris Weidman, and that loss kickstarted a 1-7 run that ended his MMA career (barring a no-contest against Nick Diaz, a win that was overturned as Silva failed a drug test). Silva’s broken leg in his rematch with Weidman offers some explanation for his severe drop-off in form, but it cannot wholly account for the skid. One of those to defeat Silva in that miserable middleweight run was Adesanya, who was 22-1, unbeaten at middleweight, and held five successful title defences before his own prime ended in a flash – almost a blur, like his trademark offence during his glory years. Adesanya’s KO by Alex Pereira marked the start of the end; although he avenged that loss with his own KO of the Brazilian five months later, the rematch seemingly showed the last vibrant flicker from a fading fighting light, because he has since lost four in a row – a points loss to seismic underdog Sean Strickland, a submission by Dricus Du Plessis, and KOs by Nassourdine Imavov and Joe Pyfer. Each of the 37-year-old’s opponents was ranked lower than the last. Usman’s decline has felt less drastic, but partly due to his lower in-ring activity, one could argue. The 39-year-old is 1-4 in his last five, like Adesanya, but the latter’s last five fights date back to April 2023, while Usman’s reach back to November 2021. When the welterweight’s 19-fight win streak (including five successful title defences) was ended by Leon Edwards’s iconic head kick, Usman was left lying on his back and sitting in the middle of a 1,316-day wait for a win. Kamaru Usman was famously knocked out cold by Leon Edwards to lose his title (Getty) That victory came in 2025, against Joaquin Buckley: a fighter of a lesser calibre than many of Usman’s recent opponents, and one who provided the right style for the former champ. Since then, Usman has fought once and lost, against Du Plessis in July. He is thus 0-2 at middleweight, thanks to a prior loss to Khamzat Chimaev, and so his bid to reinvigorate his career has failed. The declines of Silva, Usman and Adesanya came earlier in their lives than Volkanovski’s would, if it were to start now, which is testament to his longevity. Usman and Adesanya feel like relevant references because they are of the same generation; at one point, these were arguably the pound-for-pound top three fighters in MMA. It is also important to note that Volkanovski has not just staved off a sudden downfall by getting to 38 without falling apart; he has done so by actively rallying after a spell that could have marked his end. There was no shame in Volkanovski’s narrow loss to Islam Makhachev up at lightweight, and he bounced back with a masterclass against Yair Rodriguez, but when “Alexander The Great” took a rematch with Makhachev on short notice, he was knocked out in round one. His proclivity for activity looked costly, and afterwards, he admitted to struggling with his mental health when he was not fighting. Those same struggles explained his quick turnaround against Ilia Topuria four months later. Ilia Topuria stopped Volkanovski in the second round of their title fight (Getty) Topuria was a frightening contender at the time, but as well rounded as he is, his versatility is surely trumped by Volkanovski’s own. However, the Aussie’s fans feared Topuria’s sickening power specifically, and that foreboding feeling was justified when “El Matador” played the bull and trampled Volk. A fighter who had been 24-1, and who had not lost in 10 years, had suddenly lost three fights in the space of a year – including back-to-back KOs. What followed was a 14-month absence, which could have marked a needed rest or a risky move for a fighter in the latter half of his 30s, especially given his return came against the heavy-handed Diego Lopes. But Volkanovski produced a trademark clinic, with the exception of a flash knockdown from Lopes, to outpoint the Brazilian and kickstart a second title reign. Nine months later, he outpointed Lopes again, and more comfortably. That brings him to Evloev, who has patiently waited for a long-deserved title shot. Movsar Evloev (left) during a controversial decision win over Lerone Murphy in March (Getty) At 20-0 and 32 years old, he should provide a tricky test, but the wrestling specialist’s threat does not appear to resemble Lopes’s or Topuria’s; the challenger’s last three wins have been controversial decisions, and it feels like five close rounds await fans on Saturday. Many of those fans will be Evloev’s, for what that is worth; will there be a ‘home’ advantage on the scorecards? In March, the judges in London did not favour Lerone Murphy in the Britain’s tight contest with Evloev, so perhaps favouritism will be a non-factor. Still, Volkanovski will need to be at his intelligent, precise best to win the required rounds against Evloev, with whom he trained years ago . The betting odds, and MMA logic, suggest this fight will be razor close. Perhaps as close as Volk is to the edge.

item.title: Wilcox wants Howe if Manchester United sack Carrick, European reaction and more: football news – live
item.description: ⚽ All the latest news going into the weekend’s action ⚽ Premier League: weekend guide | Mail Tom In Spain, it’s the Clásico on Sunday at the Camp Nou, with leaders Barcelona having made the better start to the season, though Real Madrid – six points behind – have begun to hit their straps. But is it still the world’s biggest match? Here’s Graham Ruthven: As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico ’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico ’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture? Sunday’s match at Camp Nou will be watched by hundreds of millions of viewers all over the world. A clásico always carries significance, but this weekend’s edition will be especially significant. A Barça win would move them nine points clear of their rivals at the top of La Liga . But is it still the world’s biggest match? Here’s Graham Ruthven: As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico ’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico ’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture? Sunday’s match at Camp Nou will be watched by hundreds of millions of viewers all over the world. A clásico always carries significance, but this weekend’s edition will be especially significant. A Barça win would move them nine points clear of their rivals at the top of La Liga . A Real Madrid victory could be a catalyst for the rest of their season. Continue reading...

item.title: Mika Baur’s sobering admission – “Maybe we are not capable to win these games”
item.description: Mika Baur’s sobering admission – “Maybe we are not capable to win these games” Celtic midfielder Mika Baur has eluded that he and his teammates are maybe not capable of competing in at Europa League level… Javi Rodriguez of Real Club Celta Vigo scores his team’s first goal during the UEFA Europa League 2026/27 League Phase MD3 match between Celtic FC and Celta Vigo at Celtic Park on October 22, 2026. (Photo by Ian MacNicol/Getty Images) The £6 million summer signing from Paderborn was speaking after Celtic’s third consecutive defeat in the Europa League, after falling to a 2-1 home loss to Celta Vigo that left Celtic in the embarrassing position of being second bottom in the table. Mika Baur was Celtic’s top performer against Celta Vigo The 22 year old German international midfielder impressed once again, making his £6 million fee look like a bargain with each passing game, and scored the Celtic goal in the defeat to the mid-table La Liga side. But he’s not been shy in admitting that he and his teammates have plenty to improve on in a bid to compete on the European stage, even at the second tier level. Once again it was mightily evident that the Celtic players are under equipped for European football, despite being the dominant force in Scottish football, as young Mika was quick to point that out. He said: “The focus is performing every three days in the league. That’s first and then performing in Europa League or international football as well. Javi Rodriguez of Celta Vigo scores his team’s second goal during the UEFA Europa League 2026/27 League Phase MD3 match between Celtic FC and Celta Vigo at Celtic Park on October 22, 2026. (Photo by Ian MacNicol/Getty Images) “At the moment, maybe we are not capable to win these games.” “At the moment, maybe we are not capable to win these games. But in two weeks, that’s the next one, against Besiktas, home again. Hopefully a good atmosphere. We need the points. “But, absolutely disappointing. The first half was absolutely okay, it was an open game. Then we scored, then we had 10, 12, 15 minutes where we controlled it and dominated it, and then they scored, and at that moment the momentum switched completely and we were not capable to switch it again. “We had no control. We made mistakes, they pushed us in our own half, around our box. It’s not getting easier now, but there’s still five games ahead. What else should we do then but believe? “As I said, five games ahead and the chances are there. We need points.” HAVE YOUR SAY – Join the Celtic conversation in our comments section below… Celtic in the Fifties by Matt Corr, in two volumes, both published on 4th September 2026 by Celtic Star Books. item.title: Leclerc hits back at Hadjar's Verstappen claim: 'He has no idea what kind of car we drive'
item.description: Charles Leclerc has dismissed Isack Hadjar 's claim that Max Verstappen would have won the Singapore Grand Prix by a bigger margin in a Ferrari. Speaking on the US GP media day, the Ferrari driver called the idea "nonsense" and said nobody outside a team can judge another team's car. Finishing P2 at Marina Bay, 7.3 seconds behind Verstappen, the Monegasque driver responded to Hadjar's claims that the RB22 was not the quickest car in Singapore . "I think the car is still very hard to drive," the Frenchman said. "In Malaysia, it was dominant, but I don't think in Singapore, it was the fastest car. That's what I believe. I think if you put Max in the Ferrari, he would have won the race with more margin. So that's my opinion. In Singapore, I think it was the fastest car." Leclerc: 'I have no idea what kind of car he drives' Photo: Race Pictures Photo: Race Pictures When the comments were put to him on Thursday, Leclerc made it clear he did not think one driver can rank another team's car. He said both sides know just as little about each other. "Well, first of all, I think it's nonsense to start saying these kinds of things. Isack has no idea what kind of car we drive, and I have no idea what kind of car he drives. With a view to this weekend's US GP, Leclerc went on to say the pecking order is currently too close for anyone to call with confidence. The 29-year-old explained that the outcome at each track comes down to how well a team can extract the maximum out of its package. "I think it's such a tight field that it's very, very difficult for us to predict, Leclerc Yes, of course, we have an idea of how we will be on this track, but when you are speaking about such fine margins, it relies really on optimising your package, and that has a much bigger influence than what we expect in terms of cars." Leclerc names Mercedes as the only outlier Leclerc did single out one team. He said Mercedes had not yet shown the pace Ferrari expected from them in recent races after bringing a major upgrade at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia. Leclerc believes if they find it, they could move clear of everyone else. "I think the only outlier in the last few races is maybe Mercedes, that we expected to be further ahead than they actually were. If they manage to finally unlock the performance that we had in mind for them in the last few races, then they will be further ahead than any others. But otherwise, it's going to be very tight."

item.title: FEATURE | Bayer Leverkusen’s rise from a season of chaos
item.description: FEATURE | Bayer Leverkusen’s rise from a season of chaos Bayer Leverkusen did the unthinkable in 2023/24. They not only stopped Bayern Munich from winning the Bundesliga but also went the season unbeaten in the league to secure their maiden Meisterschale . On top of that, Xabi Alonso’s side added the DFB Pokal title to their trophy cabinet. But things began to change, especially after the Spaniard’s departure in 2025. With key players like Florian Wirtz, Jeremie Frimpong, and Granit Xhaka leaving, the team slowly fell apart. In a recent interview with The Athletic , Erik ten Hag, who arrived at the club in the summer of 2025 and was only in charge for three games, revealed that players wanted to leave. “It’s a very strange story,” he says. “They ended an era with Alonso, so all the players wanted to go. We fought for some, and they were not committed anymore. So it was waiting until September 1. The good players signed in the last couple of days. I never worked with them. Three games, and then we parted ways.” Leverkusen tried to replace the title-winning squad, but they weren’t able to achieve their goals in the 2025/26 season. The team finished sixth in the league under Kasper Hjulmand, who replaced Ten Hag. Failing to qualify for the UEFA Champions League cost the Dane his job. Carles Martinez was then appointed as head coach in June. Leverkusen sporting director Simon Rolfes stated: “Carles Martinez has successfully developed numerous young players at Toulouse and moulded an international team into a strong unit.” Rolfes added: “In addition to this valuable experience, he brings a high level of expertise from his time at the Barcelona youth academy to Leverkusen. Carles is a coach with clear principles and a modern approach to the game. We are convinced he can provide the right impetus for our sporting future.” Bayer Leverkusen’s upward trajectory The start of this season wasn’t ideal for the new coach as his team fell to a 3-2 opening day loss to newly promoted Elversberg. The alarm bells started to ring very quickly; however, in time the team managed to adapt to the coach’s demands. That loss is the only one they have suffered this season. Leverkusen have since managed to remain unbeaten in the Bundesliga and have maintained a 100 percent record in the Europa League – winning seven, and drawing one. In this run of wins, two players have stood out for Die Werkself . Patrik Schick has shrugged off his injury woes of the past to score six goals and provide two assists in six Bundesliga games this season. He also has two further goals in three Europa League games. Algerian talent Ibrahim Maza is also turning heads due to his brilliant display and output. The 20-year-old has two goals and two assists to his name in the league and has generally impressed with his skills. On comparisons to Florian Wirtz, Maza told the Bundesliga official website : “Flo is an incredible player, a real Bayer Leverkusen legend. I am still trying to follow my own path

Carles is a coach with clear principles and a modern approach to the game. I hope that one day I can play at his level and achieve that.” As Leverkusen eye a return to Europe’s elite competition, they seem to be on the right path. The team might not be able to replicate the record-breaking season from 2023/24, but recent results indicate that Leverkusen are on the right path after a season of chaos and uncertainty. item.content:encoded: Free Press sports writer Chris Solari ahead to the road trip to the Rose Bowl for Michigan State football to face Big Ten-leading No. 10 UCLA on Saturday, Oct. 24. Fast facts Matchup: Michigan State (2-5, 0-4 Big Ten) vs. No. 10 UCLA (6-0, 4-0). Kickoff: 3:30 p.m., Saturday, Oct. 24; Rose Bowl, Pasadena, California. TV/radio: CBS, WJR-AM (760). Line: Bruins by 15. JULT LIKE OLD TIMES? Pat Fitzgerald follows his old coach's wisdom to turn MSU around Michigan State football vs UCLA availability report (As of Thursday, per BigTen.org) MSU Out: LB Jordan Hall, CB Tyran Chappell, CB Charles Brantley, CB Tre Bell, CB Keshawn Williams, QB Cam Fancher, WR Charles Taplin, RB Cam Edwards, FB Jay Coyne, OL Tristan Comer, TE Joe Caudill. Questionable: QB Alessio Milivojevic, RB Jaziun Patterson, LB Brady Pretzlaff, Caleb Wheatland, LT Ben Murawski, RB Darrin Jones Jr. UCLA Out: QB Nico Iamaleava, WR Mikey Matthews, WR Jonah Smith, OL Sam Yoon, OL Jordan Davis, DB Rodrick Pleasant, DB Tao Johnson. Questionable: OL Eugene Brooks. Scouting report When MSU has the ball: The big question will be who is available for the Spartans , especially at quarterback. Alessio Milivojevic is questionable after coming off going 19-for-30 for 216 yards with two touchdown passes and another rushing score in last week’s 24-21 loss to Northwestern . (The third-year sophomore also lost a strip-sack fumble and struggled with both overthrowing open receivers and missing them in his read progression .) With Cam Fancher out, Milivojevic’s backup, freshman Kayd Coffman, is only other active QB to have played in a college game after taking 11 snaps at the end of a blowout loss at Wisconsin. Jaziun Patterson continued to run hard through contact with a 4.8-yard-per-carry average for 72 yards against the Wildcats, but he also is questionable. So is left tackle Ben Murawski, though the Spartans allowed just one sack without him against the Wildcats. MSU has scored 58 points over its past two games after scoring just 26 in three previous losses combined. The Spartans also are seeing young stars emerging, though, in the passing game with tight end Jayden Savoury and receivers Fredrick Moore and Bryson Williams. Bruins linebackers Jalen Woods and Sammy Omosigho are tied for fifth in the Big Ten with 50 tackles apiece (8.3 per game). Omosigho's 7.5 tackles for a loss rank fifth, and he and edge rusher Taylor Scott each have three of UCLA's 13 sacks. When UCLA has the ball: The Spartans will again be without three starters – linebacker Jordan Hall and cornerbacks Tre Bell and Tyran Chappell – as well as backup CB Charles Brantley. If Brady Pretzlaff and Caleb Wheatland return, that will help shore up the middle of a group that missed some critical assignments – including coverage on a checkdown on the first play of Northwestern’s eventual game-winning field goal drive – despite getting 33 combined tackles and three pass breakups from Dion Crawford and Cam Stodghill. It helped that MSU’s defensive line, led by edge rusher Anelu Lafaele and tackle Ben Roberts, generated five sacks that were the most against a Big Ten opponent since getting seven against Nebraska on Nov. 4, 2023. Roberts continues to play at an All-Big Ten level as both a run stopper and backfield disruptor. Freshman Jeremiah Favorite started at cornerback and played all 71 snaps as the Spartans held the Wildcats under both their scoring and yardage averages but failed to finish the task in the final quarter. UCLA will provide an interesting test, particularly in its second game without starting quarterback Nico Iamaleava, who suffered a season-ending knee injury against Oregon. The Bruins enter Saturday averaging 35.5 points and 445.8 yards per game, both of which rank 33rd (out of 138 FBS-level teams). Their 231 rushing yards per game lead the Big Ten and are 12th nationally, with the tandem of Wayne Knight (571 yards, 11 TDs) and Anthony Woods (347 yards, five TDs) leading the way. Former Michigan receiver Semaj Morgan is the Bruins' leading pass catcher, with 313 yards on 24 catches with two scores and is a dangerous punt returner (9.5 yards per return). Know the foe Chesney chasing: UCLA appears to be following the Indiana route, to great success, with the hiring of coach Bob Chesney away from James Madison. The 49-year-old Pennsylvania native took over the Dukes for two seasons after Curt Cignetti left for the Hoosiers and built on the success in Harrisonburg, Virginia. Chesney, who arrived from Holy Cross, went 21-6 with JMU, including 12-2 last season with a College Football Playoff appearance. The Bruins have the longest active win streak in Big Ten play, at six, and are the only league team still unbeaten this year. Stingy defense: Defensive coordinator Colin Hitschler, who followed Chesney from JMU, has UCLA playing at a high level at its season midpoint. The Bruins rank 21st nationally at 16.2 points allowed, after giving up just 25 total over their past three wins. UCLA allows just 292.3 total yards and 97.7 rushing yards per game, both of which are 20th nationally. Its 26.6% third-down defense is fifth-best, and UCLA leads the Big Ten with nine forced fumbles and 10 interceptions. Different Dieffenbach: With Iamaleava getting knocked out against Oregon, the Bruins turned to Cal Poly Ty Dieffenbach to take over the offense. The 6-foot-6, 227-pound native of nearby Calabasas, California, went 3-for-6 with the winning TD pass to Knight in a 17-15 win at Oregon, then was 22-for-33 for 264 yards with an interception (an end-of-half Hail Mary) and no touchdowns in last week’s 17-7 home win over Wisconsin. In his one season at Cal Poly, Dieffenbach (who started his college career at Pitt) completed 56.8% of his passes for 1,305 yards, nine touchdowns and nine interceptions, while adding 321 yards and four touchdowns on the ground. Chris Solari's two cents LA postcards: This is MSU’s first game at the Rose Bowl since beating Stanford there on Jan. 1, 2014. The Spartans are 4-1 all-time in the Pasadena stadium – all in "The Granddaddy of Them All," including wins there over the Bruins in the 1954 and 1956 Rose Bowl games. However, UCLA owns a 4-3 all-time record against the Spartans, including a 38-13 win to spoil MSU’s homecoming last season. The Spartans have only played the Bruins once in a regular-season road game, a 56-16 UCLA win at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on Sept. 28, 1974. Bruin bounceback: The Bruins fired alum DeShaun Foster as coach after three straight losses to open the 2025 season, then won three straight – two at home against then-No. 7 Penn State and Maryland, sandwiched around a road win at MSU on Oct. 11, 2025. UCLA, which finished 3-9 last year, was just 10-17 in Big Ten play over its first three seasons; Chesney took over this year, and the Bruins’ 4-0 mark is tied with Ohio State as the only unblemished conference records. Prediction The Spartans’ injury situation remains problematic, as they seemingly turn to the next man up behind the next man up, with a cross-country trip likely to take its toll. MSU limps into its bye week on a six-game losing streak, and potentially with a quarterback question heading into the Nov. 7 game at Michigan if Milivojevic is unable to play Saturday. The pick: UCLA 27, MSU 14. Contact Chris Solari: csolari@freepress.com . Follow him @chrissolari . Subscribe to the "Spartan Speak" podcast for new episodes weekly on Apple Podcasts , Spotify or anywhere you listen to podcasts. item.title: Is El Clásico still the world’s biggest match? Three questions before Barcelona v Real Madrid
item.description: The fixture’s relevance waned as the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded. Can Lamine Yamal and Mbappé lift it into a new era? For the best part of a decade, El Clásico was more than just soccer’s biggest fixture. It was the defining narrative. At the peak of the Lionel Messi v Cristiano Ronaldo era, there were clásicos everywhere. Yes, when the two historic rivals clashed on the pitch, but also in the voting for the Ballon d’Or every year and in so much of the discourse around the sport. As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico ’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico ’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture? Continue reading...
item.dc:creator: Graham Ruthven
item.content:encoded: The fixture’s relevance waned as the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded. Can Lamine Yamal and Mbappé lift it into a new era? For the best part of a decade, El Clásico was more than just soccer’s biggest fixture. It was the defining narrative. At the peak of the Lionel Messi v Cristiano Ronaldo era, there were clásicos everywhere. Yes, when the two historic rivals clashed on the pitch, but also in the voting for the Ballon d’Or every year and in so much of the discourse around the sport. As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico ’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico ’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture? Continue reading...

item.title: Chaotic state of football in Brazil epitomises a nation where greed has conquered glory | Jonathan Liew
item.description: The national game merely reflects the mood in a divided nation which is going to the polls with very little faith in the power of democracy Look, cards on the table: I don’t know for certain, and nor do you, whether Flávio Bolsonaro – the man widely tipped to become the next president of Brazil after Sunday night’s election – really did steal an island from Richarlison. There are lawyers involved, claims and counter-claims, and in any case, adjudicating land ownership disputes between right-wing strongmen and Tottenham reserve-team strikers lies very much beyond this column’s spectrum of expertise. It’s why, for example, this newspaper took no official position on the well-publicised battle between Rodrigo Duterte and Vincent Janssen over that Polynesian isthmus. According to Richarlison, a few years ago he purchased an island off the southern coast of Rio de Janeiro, and has the documentation to prove it. Richarlison says Bolsonaro tried to buy it from him, and when he refused a lawyer named Willer Tomaz simply turned up and annexed it. “These guys took the island without spending a penny, as far as I know,” Richarlison claimed in an Instagram video that has been viewed more than 31 million times. Tomaz has accused Richarlison of lying, arguing that he has a public deed registered at the notary’s office. Bolsonaro, for his part, has denied any connection with the island in question and described Richarlison’s intervention as “politically motivated”. Continue reading...

item.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
item.description: Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends Premier League top scorers After seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea that marked the end for Ange Postecoglou , the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing the narrow defeat by Arsenal , while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season. Niall McVeigh Ipswich v Nottingham Forest, Friday 8pm BST Aston Villa v Manchester City, Saturday 12.30pm BST Arsenal v Everton, Saturday 3pm BST Coventry v Fulham, Saturday 3pm BST Continue reading...

item.title: Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather storm
item.description: This was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. Whatever this rotten impersonation of a Milan side was, it bore no relation to those that forged such a celebrated history. The visitors resembled holograms even before their goalkeeper Mike Maignan, with an extraordinary rush of blood resulting in a penalty and red card, rendered their task impossible. They never showed the slightest hint of putting up a fight. Bournemouth simply swamped the seven-time European champions and, amid a swirling south coast storm that rarely let up, could depart singing in the rain. Amine Adli’s sumptuous late free-kick, curled left-footed from 22 yards, meant they could finish the evening with the flourish they deserved. Their joy was clear at full time and met disapproval from some of Milan’s staff, who appeared to take umbrage in a short-lived fracas near the tunnel afterwards. Continue reading...

item.title: Next in line? Main contenders for the Manchester United hot seat
item.description: With Michael Carrick’s future at Old Trafford a matter of some debate, we examine the credentials of those who could succeed him The German was of interest to Manchester City while Omar Berrada was part of the hierarchy on the other side of town. He is highly thought of and would come with an impressive CV for a 39-year-old, having taken charge of Bayern Munich and Germany. Nagelsmann is regarded as an innovator who is very demanding of his players and builds teams to press relentlessly, a concept not currently used at United, as Bruno Fernandes will testify . His spell with Germany was underwhelming, concluding with a 2026 World Cup last-32 defeat by Paraguay , and at Bayern – with an exceptional squad – he won the Bundesliga in his only full season and was sacked the following March with the team second and still in the Champions League. Continue reading...

item.title: Fifa increases preparation money for Women’s World Cup to match men’s teams
item.description: Funds for 2027 will match men’s World Cup in 2026 Players given better flights and individual hotel rooms Teams in the 2027’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil will receive the same preparation money from Fifa as those that played at the 2026 men’s tournament, the world’s governing body has announced. The preparation money for the 32 teams has been more than doubled to $2.5m (£1.86m) each. In 2023, the total preparation money for the tournament was $31m; it will now be $80m. Continue reading...

item.title: Haiti move Nations League home clash with USA to Miami amid gang violence crisis
item.description: Concacaf approves exceptional hosting arrangement Haiti to face US at Nu Stadium on 14 November Miami’s Haitian community offers home advantage Concacaf on Thursday announced it has approved Haiti’s request to relocate their Nations League quarter-final first leg against the United States on 14 November from Kingston, Jamaica, to Miami in an “exceptional hosting arrangement”. Haiti have been unable to play nominal “home” games within their borders since July 2021, with the United Nations estimating that 90% of the capital of Port-au-Prince – including the national stadium – is controlled by violent gangs. Haiti’s match, the first leg of a home-and-away series against the US, had been booked for Kingston. The Grenadiers played their 2026 World Cup qualifiers in Curaçao, Aruba and Barbados. However, the Nations League format slated Curaçao and Jamaica to host their matches on the same night as Haiti’s, shunting Haiti to Sabina Park, the home of the Jamaica national team until their current venue opened in 1962. Now a cricket ground, Sabina Park hosted two of Haiti’s Nations League qualifiers. Continue reading...

item.title: Football Daily | Post-Ferguson worn-out horror show continues at Manchester United
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! We’re in the midst of what the kids call “spooky season” – or, for our fellow fusty old-timers out there, “autumn”. If you’ve been cosying up with a few horror flicks this month, you’ll know nothing good can come from hanging around a lake at this time of year. And so it proved for Manchester United, who endured an early Halloween nightmare on the banks of Lake Como that may have driven a stake through the Michael Carrick era. Hailed as the interim anti-Amorim not so long ago, Carrick has overseen two wins this season, against Ipswich and Sabah Baku . Como were in Serie D when Carrick won Big Cup with United as a player in 2008 – now, 18 years on, he watched the Italian upstarts dance, twirl and shimmy through the set of training cones he had sent out to represent his storied club. Any chance the Independent Football Regulator could also force the sale of Manchester United while it is at it? – James Marriott. Belated birthday greetings to Florent Sinama-Pongolle, a player once described (by Big Website if memory serves) as the only footballer whose surname sounds like an art-house trend – Alan Burgess. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version, just visit this page and follow the instructions . Continue reading...

item.title: Carrick joins Wilcox under the bus after Manchester United’s latest night in crisis | Max Rushden
item.description: Bruno Fernandes followed Lisandro Martínez in revolt after his team’s 4-1 defeat to Como in the Champions League You have to credit Manchester United. Your local rivals have turned the Premier League into an almost meaningless farce. We are questioning the validity of anything we’ve seen over the past 20 years; wondering how many goals Erling Haaland will get in the Championship. We are looking at the league table from second position down and wishing we’d invested in inflatable bananas a month ago. And yet here comes the Old Trafford machine: from players to the captain to the manager to the director of football, to the director of the director of football, to a minority owner who feels the UK is being “colonised by immigrants” , to debt-leveraging majority owners who take vast sums out of the club and are collectively saying hold my Ineos-sponsored high-performance wellness immune boost smoothie. Continue reading...

item.title: Bruno Guimarães had sleepless nights before Newcastle exit but hopes for same ‘love’ at Arsenal
item.description: Midfielder says there were a lot of tears as he said goodbye at St James’ Park but he is enjoying the remorselessness at his new club For Bruno Guimarães, it was a time to show his steeliness, to fix his eyes on the prize – even if he knew it would surely mean them welling up. And then some. It was a tumultuous summer for the Brazil midfielder. A fine World Cup on a personal level was marred by a crucial penalty miss in the last-16 loss against Norway . Now he had the dream move lined up to Arsenal but it could not happen without breaking some hearts at Newcastle. Guimarães admits he lay awake at night as the emotions swirled. How could he leave Newcastle, the club where he made so many connections and enjoyed so many highs after joining from Lyon in January 2022 ? There were the Champions League qualifications and, above all, the Carabao Cup triumph in 2025 that ended a 70-year wait for a domestic trophy. On the other hand, how could he resist Arsenal and the prospect of competing regularly for the game’s top honours? Continue reading...

This autumn has seen much lobbying for the Ballon d’Or, with the Georgian a popular choice, despite his absence from the World Cup. He is expected to be out for six months, although Rodri’s comeback from serious injury – he was rested by Barcelona on Tuesday until coming off the bench in the 60th minute – shows it can take far longer than that for players to rediscover their highest level. item.title: Nottingham Forest’s false start places early focus on Glasner and Delap
item.description: Austrian’s tactics need adapting to but Forest are in the bottom three and their owner is not the patient type Sitting 19th in the Premier League was not the plan for Nottingham Forest after the arrival of a highly acclaimed manager and a £45m striker to fuel their ambitions. The fates of Oliver Glasner and Liam Delap are intertwined and with the stark stats of zero home goals and a solitary point at the City Ground it is not the dream start they were aiming for. As Delap prepares to return to Ipswich, where his career ignited, on Friday night, Forest are remaining calm. There is a desperation to get away from the short-termism that caused so many problems; 12 months ago, they were on their third head coach of a disappointing season. This summer they were ruthless with the removal of Vítor Pereira, who had done a fine job to escape the drop, because they saw an opportunity to upgrade with Glasner, hoping he could transform Forest like he did Crystal Palace. Continue reading...

item.title: Cathinka Tandberg: ‘Spurs fans hate Arsenal. That’s how it is’
item.description: Norwegian forward might look to Harry Kane for inspiration on the pitch, but when north London derby comes around, she needs no lessons on what the rivalry means “It means more than just three points. It’s for the whole club. It’s for the whole place. It’s for the whole of Tottenham.” One only needs to be in the presence of Tottenham Hotspur’s Cathinka Tandberg for a few minutes to feel the passion that emanates from her when it comes to this weekend’s north London derby. As a lifelong Spurs fan, the forward understands more than most the intensity of the rivalry that exists between her side and Arsenal, one that she cannot wait to experience once again on Saturday. “It will just be an incredible feeling,” she tells Moving the Goalposts. “I think you will feel a few nerves that you maybe don’t feel in a normal game but that’s good.” Continue reading...

But the Bayern Munich and England striker accepts the ­suspense before the big reveal at the London Palladium on Monday night is part of the show. Kane is the odds-on favourite to win the prestigious individual ­honour after a prolific run of form. The 33-year-old scored 61 goals for Bayern last season and 12 for England. This time out, he has 10 for Bayern and six for England. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘We can go all the way’: Jonas Eidevall on life at San Diego Wave and lessons learned from Arsenal
item.description: The Swede’s team are second in the NWSL and hope to create special memories at their Snapdragon Stadium “I love the ocean,” Jonas Eidevall says, and he references walks along the beach at Del Mar. “People are very relaxed, life is lived at a slower pace here. I’m a very simple person. I like to read a book, go to the gym and spend time with my wife and kids, that’s sort of all I need.” The former Arsenal head coach is revelling in a calmer world as the head coach of San Diego Wave but it is not merely the beaches that are lowering his stress levels; his team are on a five-game winning streak in the NWSL and sit second in the table, one point off top spot, with two matches to go before the playoffs. Winning feels good and the club are targeting silverware, as he tells the Guardian: “It would mean everything. There are no guarantees in the playoffs, but the exciting part is saying: ‘We can also go all the way’ – that’s a possibility for us and we need to believe.” Continue reading...

item.title: Manchester City have been a joy to watch but they became detached from their roots | Philipp Lahm
item.description: City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward Do we have to reassess Manchester City now? In my columns, I have repeatedly engaged with this club and its key figures. Looking back at what I have written over the years, I believe it remains beyond question that the team have achieved greatness. I always loved watching them: they were a true unit on the pitch, a finely tuned orchestra. I would also write all over again that the conductor, Pep Guardiola, masters his craft like few others. I could recognise his teams even if they were wearing the wrong shirts and the game was broadcast in black and white – by the passes, the distances between the players and the intelligence of their interplay. It is no wonder Guardiola inspires others to become managers; look at Vincent Kompany, Mikel Arteta, Enzo Maresca, and perhaps some time Ilkay Gündogan and Rodri. Continue reading...

item.title: Does anyone feature on more than two clubs' all-time top-10 scoring charts? | The Knowledge
item.description: Plus: the longest kit supply partnerships, more own goals (part II) and consecutive goalless draws Mail us with all of your questions and answers “Harry Kane is now Bayern’s seventh-highest scorer of all time, as well as being Tottenham’s highest scorer. The man he overtook at the top of that list, Jimmy Greaves, is also Chelsea’s seventh-highest scorer of all time. Do any other players feature on two (or more) clubs’ all-time top- 10 scoring charts?” asks Owen Powell. A trawl through the Knowledge archive reminded us that we have previously looked at players who are the record goalscorer for more than one club . This question is slightly different, as we’re focusing on goalscorers who are in the all-time top 10 for the most different clubs. There are dozens of players who appear for two clubs, including Sergio Ag üero (Atlético Madrid and Manchester City), Kenny Dalglish (Celtic and Liverpool), Jimmy Greaves (Chelsea and Tottenham) , Lionel Messi (Barcelona and Inter Miami), Cristiano Ronaldo (Real Madrid and Al-Nassr) and Alan Shearer (Blackburn and Newcastle). Continue reading...

item.title: Too much Overlap? Gary Neville’s podcast empire knows no bounds
item.description: The Overlap has gone daily, with Steven Gerrard and Joe Hart among the latest additions to an ever-growing family Viewed in 2026, Nathan Barley, Chris Morris’s 2005 sitcom, shows remarkable prescience about the last two decades of metropolitan life, from smartphone addiction and digital derangement to sheer existential vapidity. When Barley’s character referred to his occupation as “self-facilitating media node”, Morris and co-writer Charlie Brooker were way ahead on the creator economy. What the pair failed to predict was ex-footballers joining the sector in droves. These days, if you are a former footballer without a podcast or YouTube channel, then did you ever really play the game? Setting aside the Gary Lineker Goalhanger empire, manspreading its centrist-dad agenda into issues way beyond guffaws with Micah Richards and Alan Shearer, there is Gary Neville to rule them all. Manchesterism’s second-most influential practitioner has been on heavy manoeuvres. Unlike Lineker’s productions, the Overlap’s output continues to stick largely to football; a rugby podcast was mothballed in February, though its cricket equivalent continues. Continue reading...

item.title: Dwight Yorke: ‘I’m not a kid trying to get into management – I’m a manager’
item.description: Ghana may soon come calling for Trinidad and Tobago’s former captain and manager, who is proud of his CV since his days as a Premier League striker Dwight Yorke wants you to stop calling him a former player. “I’m not a kid trying to get into management for the first time,” he says from his home in Dubai. “I’ve done that and I want that message to come across clearly.” The message has a deadline. Carlos Queiroz left his job as Ghana head coach on 1 October and the Ghana Football Association is searching for his successor. Yorke is among the names under consideration, along with Pape Thiaw, Aliou Cissé and Walid Regragui, the former Morocco head coach, according to Ghanaian media. Continue reading...

item.title: Will that do? Lamine Yamal conjures another magical spell as Barça pass first test | Sid Lowe
item.description: The 19-year-old scored a cracker in Seville, days after his ‘almost rabona’ at Galatasaray, as La Liga leaders beat Real Betis When at last it was time for Lamine Yamal to leave, the 19-year-old’s number going up before the 90th minute for only the second time since the opening day, Real Betis fans whistled him all the way to the touchline where Barcelona’s coach was waiting. His work here was done, Hansi Flick invited him to take the weight off his feet and his shoulders, not that he wanted to. First, though, he took Lamine Yamal’s head in his hands and, leaning in away from the amateur lip readers, tried to make himself heard over the noise. “I told him I was proud of him because he played a fantastic game,” he said. At least he could think of something. When Lamine Yamal had opened the scoring just nine minutes into the match that was supposed to find out how good Barcelona really were, it hadn’t been easy. Nothing erudite, anyway. On the morning that Barcelona went to Betis – first v third, a proper opponent at last – Jorge Valdano had lamented that sometimes he doesn’t have the words, and he always has the words. Valdano had just watched Lamine do that , whatever that was , in Istanbul – an “almost rabona ”, the kid called it – and now he had a problem. “If he keeps doing strange things, we’re not going to be able to explain it,” he wrote . Continue reading...

item.title: Houdini act in Venice leaves Massimiliano Allegri searching for an escape at Napoli | Nicky Bandini
item.description: Manager’s latest setback exposed growing doubts about his squad and his approach as Davide Nicola began his Venezia tenure with a remarkable win “I’ll love you even if you win,” promised the Venezia supporter’s banner. More gallows humour from a fanbase that proved long ago that its relationship with the club could survive a defeat. They had endured six already in the first six rounds of this Serie A season: the only team in the division without a win or even a single point. The last time they were in Serie A, in 2024-25, Venezia finished 19th. The time before that, in 2021-22, they finished bottom. Deja vu all over again? A 3-1 defeat by Atalanta in the first game back after this month’s international break pushed Venezia to breaking point. The club fired the manager Giovanni Stroppa, who had led them to the Serie B title and promotion the previous season. Continue reading...

item.title: Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: Diego Gómez’s wondergoal in a five-star demolition is just the latest in an impressive run of results for the south coast team Sign up for our free newsletter here For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes. This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League? Continue reading...

item.title: WSL talking points: pressure mounts on Slegers as Hemp closes on record
item.description: Another round of games and another disappointing draw for Arsenal while Manchester City sit top of the table with a 100% record There would have been hope that the international break could offer the Arsenal players and staff a reset but the same problems reared their head at the Emirates on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Birmingham. As they have done so often this season, the Gunners dominated most attacking and possession-based metrics – they registered 76% possession, a 2.73 xG and 43 touches in the opposition box – but their profligacy in front of goal and lack of urgency in their play once again came to the fore. Of their 27 chances, they managed just four on target as they toiled against a resilient opposition who understood the playbook. Birmingham set up in a strong defensive structure, protecting their box admirably with numbers to frustrate Renée Slegers’s side, who famously struggle to break down low blocks. In contrast, Birmingham scored with their one shot on target as Océane Hurtré took her impressive tally to six in six. Sophie Downey Match report: Arsenal 1-1 Birmingham Continue reading...

item.title: Elite-level incompetence is Manchester United’s problem – not Michael Carrick | Barney Ronay
item.description: Getting rid of head coach is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something different At the final whistle at Elland Road the TV cameras cut to a lingering shot of the Manchester United chief executive, Omar Berrada, looking down pensively from the stands, deciding, it is to be hoped, on a little clemency, a re-sheathing of the managerial shotgun. Here we have the man who hired the man. The man who fires the man. The man who also hired or rehired the previous two men he had to fire. Berrada was poached from Manchester City on the basis of his ability to grow commercial revenue (yes, OK, stop laughing), and appears, like everyone else with any actual reach around here, to exist in a strangely consequence-free bubble. Continue reading...

Berrada was poached from Manchester City on the basis of his ability to grow commercial revenue (yes, OK, stop laughing), and appears, like everyone else with any actual reach around here, to exist in a strangely consequence-free bubble. Continue reading...

item.title: Europe is a blast – but more a curse than a blessing if you are not a Premier League super-club I Jonathan Wilson
item.description: The four Premier League clubs playing in the lesser continental competitions face each other on Sunday – but three are struggling domestically The sun shone. The temperature was in the high 20s. There was a mood of great conviviality. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free. Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.” Continue reading...

item.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
item.description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.” Continue reading...

item.title: Martínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownership | Jonathan Liew
item.description: Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the club Heartbreaking: the worst defender you know just made a great point. And no, nobody would describe Lisandro Martínez as the ideal person to scrutinise Manchester United’s indifferent start to the season , given that his high-profile defensive errors against Fulham and Tottenham are partly responsible for it. “We’re all trying to find the guy who did this,” Martínez burbles on Amazon Prime after United’s 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid on Tuesday night, dressed in a hot dog costume and throwing his arms out in mock innocence. For those with no interest in engaging with what Martínez actually had to say, this alone will be sufficient grounds to ignore him. Already you can sense the squeamishness of former players for whom the violation of an omertà is the real cardinal sin here, a phantom limb that still tingles years after they last stepped into a dressing room. “Disrespectful,” reckoned Wayne Rooney. “I don’t feel like he’s got the right,” agreed Ashley Young. “These things don’t end well, man,” Rio Ferdinand observed on his podcast. Continue reading...

item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. Continue reading...

item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. Ed Aarons Continue reading...

item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game. Continue reading...

item.title: Sign up for the Moving the Goalposts newsletter: our free women’s football email
item.description: Get our roundup of women’s football for free twice a week, featuring the insights of experts such as Ada Hegerberg and Magdalena Eriksson Join us as we delve deeper into the wonderful world of women’s football in our weekly newsletter. It is informative, entertaining, global, critical – when needed – and, above all, passionate. Written mainly by Júlia Belas Trindade and Sophie Downey , expect guest appearances from stars such as Anita Asante, Ada Hegerberg and many more. Try our other sports emails: as well as the occasionally funny football email The Fiver from Monday to Friday, there are weekly catch-ups for cricket in The Spin and rugby union in The Breakdown , and our seven-day roundup of the best of our sports journalism in The Recap .
